**EMVCo drafts framework for card-based agentic payments**

*A first attempt by the card industry's technical body to set interoperability standards for AI agents making payments on behalf of consumers, the draft framework aims to prevent fragmentation before the market scales.*

EMVCo has published a draft framework designed to promote secure, interoperable and scalable card-based agentic payments. The document, now open for industry feedback, addresses how AI agents can initiate and authorise card transactions while maintaining the security guarantees that underpin EMV specifications.

Agentic payments – where software agents transact autonomously on a user's behalf – have moved rapidly from concept to early production in 2026. Visa and Mastercard have both launched agentic programmes, and card-based agentic pilots have appeared in Europe through ING, Worldline and Credit Agricole. But card-based agentic payments have lacked a shared technical specification, leaving individual schemes and processors to define their own approaches.

EMVCo's intervention is an effort to prevent fragmentation before the market scales. By proposing a common framework now, the body is signalling that card networks intend to compete for agentic commerce rather than cede the space to account-to-account or stablecoin alternatives. The feedback period will shape how authentication, liability and consent are handled when no human is present at the point of sale.

*Sources: [EMVCo reqests feedback on framework for card-based agentic payments](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110761/emvco-reqests-feedback-on-framework-for-card-based-agentic-payments?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra | [EMVCo reqests feedback on framework for card-based agentic payments](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110760/emvco-reqests-feedback-on-framework-for-card-based-agentic-payments?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Singapore proposes legislation to regulate stablecoins under payments law**

*The consultation would embed existing stablecoin regulatory requirements into statute, giving Singapore one of the first comprehensive legislative regimes for the asset class.*

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has published a consultation paper proposing amendments to the Payment Services Act 2019 that would give its stablecoin regulatory framework the force of legislation. MAS introduced administrative guidelines for stablecoins in 2023 and has since operated a licensing regime; the proposed changes would codify reserve, redemption and disclosure requirements directly in law.

The move comes as jurisdictions compete to set the regulatory baseline for stablecoins. The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation has been in force since mid-2024, and the UK is developing its own regime following the Bank of England's consultation on systemic stablecoins. In US federal legislation, stablecoins remain stalled. Singapore's approach – upgrading an existing administrative framework into statute – offers a model that avoids starting from scratch while providing the legal certainty issuers and institutional users require.

For European payments professionals, the consultation is relevant on two fronts. Singapore is a major hub for cross-border stablecoin settlement, with Visa already piloting stablecoin projects there. And the legislative architecture MAS proposes – anchoring stablecoin rules within existing payments law rather than creating a standalone regime – mirrors the approach several European regulators have considered for integrating digital assets into existing frameworks.

*Sources: [Singapore central bank proposes legislative framework for stablecoins](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/110762/singapore-central-bank-proposes-legislative-framework-for-stablecoins?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Danmarks Nationalbank governor makes resilience case for PSD3 implementation**

*Ulrik Noedgaard's speech positions operational resilience – not innovation – as the central concern for Denmark's approach to the next payments directive.*

Ulrik Noedgaard, governor of Danmarks Nationalbank, has delivered a speech on PSD3 and open banking that frames operational resilience as the defining priority for the next phase of European payments regulation. Speaking at a PSD3 and open banking conference on August 31, Noedgaard set out the Danish central bank's perspective on how resilient payment infrastructure should be maintained as the regulatory framework evolves.

The speech arrives as PSD3 negotiations continue through the European legislative process and as Denmark's own payments landscape faces particular pressures. Denmark's participation in the ECB's cross-currency instant payments pilot, launched in June, links its krone-denominated system to euro area infrastructure – creating new interdependencies that make resilience questions more concrete than they might be for a purely eurozone member.

Central bankers across Europe have increasingly emphasised resilience alongside innovation in payments policy. The Bank of Finland framed payment autonomy as a geopolitical imperative earlier this year, and the UK government has added a payments innovation mandate to the Bank of England's remit. Noedgaard's intervention adds a Nordic voice to a debate that has been dominated by eurozone and UK perspectives, and underscores that PSD3's operational requirements may matter as much as its data-sharing provisions for the countries that must implement it.

*Sources: [Governor Ulrik Nødgaard's presentation at PSD3 & Open Banking](https://www.nationalbanken.dk/en/news-and-knowledge/publications-and-speeches/speeches/2026/governor-ulrik-noedgaards-presentation-at-psd3-open-banking-resilient-payments-from-danmarks-nationalbanks-point-of-view) — Danmarks Nationalbank*

stories.original:
**TD Bank completes tokenised payment using Project Agora platform**

*Real US dollar funds have moved through the BIS-backed multi-currency tokenisation platform, advancing the project from prototype to live settlement.*

TD Bank has carried out a tokenised payment moving real US dollar funds through Project Agora, the Bank for International Settlements-backed platform exploring how tokenised commercial bank deposits can interoperate with wholesale central bank money for cross-border settlement. The transaction marks a progression from the proof-of-concept stage that the BIS reported on in March.

Project Agora brings together seven central banks – including the Banque de France, Bank of Korea and the Swiss National Bank – with a consortium of private-sector financial institutions. The platform tests whether tokenised deposits, held on a shared ledger, can settle cross-border payments more efficiently than correspondent banking. TD's transaction demonstrates that the infrastructure can handle real value, not just test tokens.

The European dimension is direct. The Banque de France and Swiss National Bank are both participants, and the project's design principles overlap with the ECB's own work on wholesale settlement using distributed ledger technology (DLT). The Bank of England's 2025 assessment, published in May, found "significant trade-offs" in DLT for wholesale settlement; Agora's incremental progress with real funds offers a counterpoint to that caution and will inform European policy decisions on whether tokenised settlement belongs in production infrastructure.

*Sources: [TD tests tokenised payments through Project Agorá](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48326/td-tests-tokenised-payments-through-project-agor?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
